summary
Background & aims: Dietary intake of several speci ﬁc macronutrients have been linked to risk of coro-
nary heart disease (CHD). However, this association may depend on overall macronutrient composition
rather than one single macronutrient. Therefore, we aimed to investigate the associations of macronu-
trient intake and CHD and its related risk factors, by taking into account different macronutrient
substitutions.
Methods: This study was performed in 5873 participants from the Rotterdam Study, a population-based
cohort study. Macronutrient intake was measured using a semi-quantitative food frequency question-
naire (FFQ). Cox proportional hazard regression analyses were used to examine the association between
intakes of macronutrients and CHD incidence; and linear regression analyses were used to examine the
associations with the related risk factors, including triglycerides, total, high-density and low-density
cholesterol levels, body mass index (BMI), fat mass index (FMI), and fat-free mass index (FFMI).
Results: We documented 669 CHD cases, during 74,776 person-years of follow-up. In multivariable-
adjusted models we observed no signi ﬁcant associations between macronutrients and CHD incidence.
Although non-signi ﬁcant, a higher plant protein intake tended to be associated with a lower risk of CHD
at the expense of all other macronutrients, and this association was strongest when 5% of energy (5 En%)
of plant protein was consumed at the expense of animal protein (HR ¼ 0.61; 95% CI 0.31, 1,21), mono- and
disaccharides (HR ¼ 0.62; 95% CI 0.29, 1.35) and saturated fat (HR ¼ 0.61; 95% CI 0.31, 1.20). No consistent
associations were observed for risk factors related to CHD.
Conclusions: Macronutrient composition was not signi ﬁcantly associated with CHD incidence or car-
diometabolic risk factors in an adult population. Future studies should further investigate food sources
and quality of macronutrients.

1. Introduction
Macronutrient intake has been linked to many chronic dis-
eases, including coronary heart disease (CHD). However, con-
ﬂicting results have been reported on associations of protein, fat,
and carbohydrate intake with CHD incidence and risk factors
related to CHD, such as lipid levels and body composition [ 1e4]. To
interpret health effects of any dietary component, but especially
for macronutrients, it is crucial to take into account effects of
energy intake and overall macronutrient composition of the diet
[5]. A higher intake of one macronutrient in an isocaloric diet
involves a lower intake of another macronutrient. For instance,
within the Alpha-Tocopherol, Beta-Carotene Cancer Prevention
Study 21,955 male smokers between 50 and 69 years a

replacement of saturated fatty acids (SFA) and trans-fat with
carbohydrates showed a decreased risk for CHD, whereas the
replacement of mono-unsaturated fatty acids (MUFA) with car-
bohydrates resulted in an increased risk [ 6]. Similar results were
obtained for protein and carbohydrate substitutions. In a pro-
spective cohort study following 29,017 postmenopausal women
from Iowa for 15 years an isoenergetic replacement of carbohy-
drates or animal protein by vegetable protein was associated with
a 30% decreased CHD mortality among women with the highest
protein intake [ 7]. These results suggest that distinction between
subgroups of macronutrients should be made as substitution as-
sociations may differ, such as for animal protein and vegetable
protein.
Hence, the macronutritional balance of the diet rather than
single macronutrients should be examined when studying the as-
sociation between macronutrients and CHD risk. Nevertheless, to
date no studies have been conducted on all macronutrients and
their substitutions in relation to CHD risk. Therefore, we aimed to
comprehensively investigate the relation of macronutrient intake
with CHD and its risk factors, including lipid levels and measures of
body composition, by taking into account macronutrient sub-
stitutions in this association in participants free of cardiometabolic
diseases at baseline.
2. Methods
2.1. The Rotterdam Study
The current analyses were embedded in the Rotterdam study,
a population-based prospective cohort study in the city of Rot-
terdam, the Netherlands [ 8]. The ﬁrst cohort started in 1990 (RS-
I) and included participants of 55 years or over, living in the well-
deﬁned Ommoord district of Rotterdam. Until September 1993 all
residents of this suburb matching the criteria (n ¼ 10,215) were
invited and 7983 people responded (response of 78%). In 2000 a
second cohort (RS-II) started with persons that became 55 years
or those of 55 years or over that migrated into this district since
the start of the study. Of the initially 4472 invited persons, 301 1
responded (response of 67%). A further extension of the study
(RS-III) was initiated in 2006, of the 6057 invited subjects aged
45e54 years, 3932 responded (65% response). In total 14,926
subjects are included in the Rotterdam study, with an overall
response of 72%. Brie ﬂy, examinations of the participants were
administered at baseline enrollment including a home interview
(2 h) by a trained research assistant and physical examinations
(5 h) at the research center in their district. The Rotterdam Study
has been approved by the Medical Ethics Committee of the
Erasmus MC (registration number MEC 02.1015) and by the Dutch
Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport (Population Screening Act
WBO, license number 1071272-159521-PG). The Rotterdam
Study has been entered into the Netherlands National Trial
Register (NTR; www.trialregister.nl ) and into the WHO Interna-
tional Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP; www.who.int/
ictrp/network/primary/en/ )u n d e rs h a r e dc a t a l o g u en u m b e r
NTR6831. All participants provided written informed consent to
participate in the study and to have their information obtained
from treating physicians [ 8].
2.2. Study population
Of all 14,926 participants at baseline, we had complete di-
etary data available for 9701 participants (5433 from RS-I, 1624
from RS-II, and 2644 from RS-III) [ 9]. From this group, we
additionally excluded 3828 subjects because of history of CHD,
stroke, or diabetes mellitus at baseline as diet may change in
response to these events, or missing follow-up data, or no
informed consent, which left 5873 participants for current an-
alyses ( Fig. 1 ).
2.3. Dietary data
Dietary intake of all macronutrients and their respective sub-
types, including total protein, animal protein, plant protein, total
carbohydrate, mono- and disaccharides, polysaccharides, total fat,
SFA, MUFA, and poly-unsaturated fatty acid (PUFA), were assessed
at baseline using validated FFQs [9]. Dietary intake for RS-I and RS-II
was assessed in a two-step approach. Participants completed a self-
administered questionnaire about the type of food and drinks
consumed at least twice a month during the preceding year, as well
as about dietary habits, supplement use and prescribed diets. Based
on these data, subjects underwent a standardized interview su-
pervised by a trained dietitian during their next visit in the research
center after completing a checklist about their nutritional intake
using 170-item semi-quantitative FFQ to assess the amount and
frequency in times per day, week, or month of their nutritional
intake. The FFQ included 13 food groups and additional questions
on prescribed diets, supplementary use, dietary habits and took
seasonal variations in fruit, vegetable, and ﬁsh intakes into account
[7]. In RS-III, subjects completed a self-administered more
comprehensive FFQ containing of 389 items, based on a validated
FFQ for Dutch adults [ 10,11]. Portion sizes in both FFQs were
expressed in standardized household measures (e.g., spoon or cup)
and natural units (e.g., piece of fruit or slice of bread). To derive total
energy and nutrient intakes per day the food intake data were
linked to the Dutch Food Composition Table of 1993 for RS-I, 2001
for RS-II, and 2006 for RS-III [ 12e14]. Both FFQs have been exten-
sively evaluated e against repeated food records, dietary histories,
and for protein intake against 24 h urinary urea e which consis-
tently showed that the FFQs are able to rank participants according
to their intake. FFQ's were validated for macronutrients and sub-
types of macronutrients, for which Pearson's correlations ranged
between 0.61 and 0.83 [ 10,11,15].

2.4. Ascertainment of CHD
The primary endpoint of this study was incident CHD after the
standardized home interview of each individual participant at
baseline. CHD was de ﬁned as a fatal or non-fatal myocardial
infarction (MI), a surgical or percutaneous myocardial revasculari-
zation procedure, or CHD mortality [ 16]. Information on incident
CHD was obtained through automated linkage of the study data-
base to medical reports of general practitioners and hospitals in the
research area. Data from participants with general practitioners
outside the study area was obtained through annual collection of
their medical records. All data on potential events were indepen-
dently adjudicated by two research physicians and subsequently
reviewed by a medical specialist in cardiovascular disease, whose
judgment was considered decisive. Follow-up information for CHD
was available until January 1, 2015.
2.5. Assessment of CHD risk factors
CHD risk factors, including body composition, triglycerides, and
total, low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol, and high-density
lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol were analyzed as secondary out-
comes. These aspects of cardiometabolic health were measured at
the research center at baseline and during follow-up visits (RSI-5,
RSII-3, and RSIII-2). Height and weight of the participants were
obtained during physical examinations at the research center while
wearing indoor clothes without shoes. Body mass index (BMI) was
calculated as weight divided by height squared (kg/m 2). Total lean
and fat mass were assessed using whole-body DXA in all cohorts
from the 2002 follow-up onwards, from which fat mass index (FMI)
and fat-free mass index (FFMI) was calculated. Fasting blood sam-
ples were obtained for all sub-cohorts in which we assessed con-
centrations of triglycerides, and total, LDL and HDL cholesterol with
an automated enzymatic method using Roche CHODPAP reagent
agent [16e18].
2.6. Assessment of covariates
Information on covariates was collected during home interviews
or was measured at the study center visit at baseline. Educational
level of the subjects was self-reported and categorized as low
(primary education), intermediate (secondary general or vocational
education), or high (higher vocational education or university).
Smoking behavior was classi ﬁed as never, former, or current. Data
on physical activity were obtained through an adapted version of
the Zutphen Physical Activity Questionnaire for RSI and RSII, and
the LASA Physical Activity Questionnaire for RSIII [ 19,20], from
which we calculated METh/week þ z-scores per cohort. Informa-
tion on prevalent diseases was obtained during the standardized
home interview and reviewed by a study physician using medical
records, during physical examinations at the research center and
through linkage with data from the Nationwide Medical Registry
(LMR, Utrecht, the Netherlands) [ 16]. Current medication use was
assessed during the home interview and was coded in accordance
with the Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical (ATC) classi ﬁcation
system. Blood pressure was measured in duplicate at the right
brachial artery using a random-zero sphygmomanometer with the
participant sitting quietly for at least 5 min. The mean of both
measurements was calculated. Participants were categorized as
hypertensive when they had a systolic blood pressure /C21 140 mmHg,
and/or a diastolic blood pressure /C21 90 mmHg, and/or use of anti-
hypertensive medication.
2.7. Statistical analyses
To assess the associations of macronutrient intake with risk of
CHD, cox proportional hazards regression was used. Person years
were calculated starting from the date of baseline examinations
until January 1, 2015, or ﬁrst CHD event, last contact or death.
Energy percentage of the macronutrients in total, as well as their
subgroups, were included in the analysis. In order to account for
confounding effects of total energy intake and substitutional in-
ﬂuences of other macronutrients nutrient density substitution
models were created [ 21]. In these models intakes of all nutrients
that contribute to the total amount of energy intake were
included, except for one. Intakes were expressed per 5% of total
energy intake (5 En%) and included in the same model, at the
expense of one nutrient (i.e. the nutrient left out of the model).
Therefore, coef ﬁcients can be interpreted as a 5 E% higher intake
at the expense of the nutrient left out. Hazard ratios (HRs) were
calculated with 95% con ﬁdence intervals (CI) for CHD incidence.
Subsequently, models were adjusted for several potential con-
founders based on previous literature, including total energy
intake, age, sex, study cohort, education, smoking, physical ac-
tivity, baseline BMI, hypertension, lipid reducing medication, and
ﬁber intake. Linear regression analyses adjusted for the same
covariates was used to investigate the associations between
macronutrient intake and triglycerides, total cholesterol, LDL
cholesterol, HDL cholesterol, BMI, FMI, and FFMI, for which
follow-up measurements were used. Furthermore, to examine
whether associations of macronutrient intake with CHD or its risk
factors differed by sex, age, or BMI, interaction terms were
included in the models. A p < 0.05 (two-sided) was considered
statistically signi ﬁcant. In order to reduce bias due to missing data
and increase statistical power multiple imputation (n ¼ 10 im-
putations) was implemented using the predictive mean matching
method. Percentages of missing data and characteristics of
imputed covariates are presented in
Supplemental Table 1 .N o n -
linearity of associations was explored for all analyses using
spline models. All analyses were executed with IBM SPSS Statistics
for Windows, version 21.0, software (IBM Corporation, Armonk,
New York) and R version 3.4.1 (The R Foundation for Statistical
Computing, Vienna, Austria).
3. Results
Characteristics of the study population are presented in
Table 1. Mean age of the population was 61.6 ± 7.9 years, and the
majority was female (60.8%). We documented 669 CHD cases,
during 74,776 person-years of follow-up (mean person years of
follow-up was 12.7 ± 6.6). Mean energy intake was
2133 ± 622 kcal/d. Mean intake of total protein was 16.3 ± 2.9 E%,
of which the majority was animal protein (10.2 ± 3.1 E%). Mean
total intake of carbohydrate was 43.8 ± 7.1 E%. Subtypes of car-
bohydrate intake was equally distributed, intake of mono- and
disaccharides was 22.2 ± 4.7 E% and intake of polysaccharides
was 21.6 ± 6.4 E%. Mean total fat intake was 34.7 ± 6.6 E%, of
which 13.1 ± 3.3 E% was SFA, 1 1.7 ± 2.8 E% was MUFA, and
7.0 ± 2.4 E% PUFA. Supplemental Table 2 shows population
characteristics and macronutrient intakes across the three sub-
cohorts of the Rotterdam Study. Mean age was higher for RS-I
(65.32 ± 6.74 y) and RS-II (62.82 ± 7.64 y) compared to RS-III
(56.65 ± 6.28 y). Energy intake was higher in RSIII
(2308.5 ± 713.7) compared to RSI and RSII (1983.4 ± 503.4 and
2149.7 ± 592.9, respectively), however relative intake of all
macronutrients was similar across cohorts.
Table 2 shows the results for the Cox models on association of
macronutrient intake with CHD. Overall, we observed no

statistically signiﬁcant associations between macronutrient intake
and CHD risk. However, albeit non-signi ﬁcant, we observed
consistent associations for higher intake of plant protein intake
when consumed at the expense of all other macronutrients with a
lower risk of CHD, for which associations were most pronounced at
the expense of animal protein (HR ¼ 0.69; 95% CI 0.38, 1,23), mono-
and disaccharides (HR ¼ 0.70; 95% CI 0.36, 1.36) and saturated fat
(HR ¼ 0.67; 95% CI 0.38, 1.20).
In additional analysis we examined macronutrient intake in
relation to CHD risk factors, such as triglycerides, total cholesterol,
LDL cholesterol, HDL cholesterol, BMI, FMI, and FFMI. Supplemental
table 3-9 shows the ﬁndings on associations of macronutrients and
these CHD risk factors. No consistent associations were observed
for triglycerides, total cholesterol, LDL-cholesterol, and HDL-
cholesterol. Furthermore, no statistically signi ﬁcant associations
were observed for BMI, FMI, FFMI. No non-linearity was observed in
any of the spline models. Furthermore, none of the interaction
terms for sex, age, or BMI were signi ﬁcant.
4. Discussion
In this population-based study among 5873 Dutch persons aged
45 or older, no signi ﬁcant associations were observed between
macronutrient intake and risk of CHD. We also did not observe any
consistent associations with cardiometabolic risk factors, including
BMI, FMI, FFMI, triglycerides, total cholesterol, LDL-cholesterol, and
HDL-cholesterol.
To our knowledge, this is the ﬁrst study that applied a
comprehensive substitution approach for all macronutrients and its
subtypes in relation to CHD incidence and related cardiometabolic
risk factors. There has been one study examining macronutrient
composition in relation to coronary artery calci ﬁcation (CAC)
among over 10,000 Korean adults. In line with our ﬁndings, no
association was observed between different macronutrients and
CAC [ 22]. Our ﬁndings are in line with a few previous studies
investigating single macronutrients in relation to CHD or risk fac-
tors related to CHD which also reported null ﬁndings. In the ARIC
study, also no signiﬁcant associations were observed between total,
plant, or animal protein and CHD [2]. Even though we did not ﬁnd a
statistically signi ﬁcant association for different types of protein
with CHD, we did observe consistent inverse associations for plant
protein and CHD, although non-signi ﬁcant. A high plant protein
intake could re ﬂect a higher plant-based diet in general. Since a
higher plant-based diet has previously been shown to be associated
with a lower risk of CHD [ 23], this observed trend could therefore
be attributable to a higher plant-based diet.
In agreement with our results, a previous study conducted in
the Nurses' Health Study and Health Professionals Follow-up
Study also reported no signi ﬁcant associations between carbo-
hydrate intake and CHD [ 24]. It is suggested that quality of car-
bohydrate may be more important that quantity, such as ﬁber
ratio. Furthermore, the Singapore Chinese Health Study and the
PURE study also did not ﬁnd an association between carbohydrate
intake and CHD [ 25,26]. In contrast, within the Shanghai Men's
and Women's Health Study participants with the highest quartile
of daily carbohydrate intake had an increased risk of CHD
compared to participants in the lowest quartile [ 25]. In line with
this, in a cross-sectional study within the Framingham Offspring
Participants, a higher intake of carbohydrates was unfavorably
associated with cardiometabolic risk factors, i.e. HDL-cholesterol
and triglycerides [ 27].
In contrast to the present study, a reduced risk of CHD was
observed when replacing saturated fat by PUFAs in a pooled anal-
ysis of 1 1 European and American cohort studies, which analyzed
the association of MUFAs, PUFAs and carbohydrates with CHD [ 28].
Another study combining data from the Nurses' Health Study
following 84,628 women and Health Professionals Follow-up Study
following 42,908 men took different sources of carbohydrates into
account and found that both PUFAs and high-quality carbohydrates
are associated with a decreased risk of CHD if they replace dietary
saturated fat [ 29].
In our current study, we did not observe any signi ﬁcant asso-
ciations between intake of macronutrients and cardiometabolic
risk factors, such as cholesterol levels and triglycerides. This is in
contrast with a few previous studies that did observe an associ-
ation. In the OmniHeart study, a randomized trial among adults, a
diet high in protein compared to carbohydrate was associated
with lower levels of LDL-cholesterol, HDL-cholesterol, and tri-
glyceride [ 30]. In the same study, it was observed that a diet high
in PUFA compared to carbohydrate was associated with higher
levels of HDL-cholesterol and lower levels of triglycerides [ 30].
Similarly, among participants from the Whitehall II Study, higher
intake of PUFA was associated with lower levels of triglycerides as
well as LDL-cholesterol [ 31]. Contradicting results have been re-
ported for carbohydrate intake. A study among Korean adults re-
ported that higher carbohydrate intake was associated with
higher levels of HDL-cholesterol [ 32], whereas in the Whitehall II
Study higher intake of carbohydrate was associated with lower
levels of HDL as well as lower BMI, LDL-cholesterol, and triglyc-
eride levels [ 31].

with extensive data collection, allowing the adjustment for many

possible confounders and a long follow-up period. Furthermore,
a major strength of our study was the use of substitution models
that combines all macronutrients in association with CHD inci-
dence. Substitution models allowed us to examine whether as-
sociations would be different when one of the macronutrients
was substituted for different macronutrients, as well as their
respective subtypes [ 21]. A limitation of this study is the obser-
vational nature, therefore, no causal relationship can be
concluded. Furthermore, residual confounding cannot be ruled
out, as in any observational study. Moreover, using an FFQ relies
on self-report and can lead to measurement error. Therefore, it
may not have been possible to estimate accurate absolute
amounts of nutritional intakes. Nevertheless, this instrument has
been shown to be an appropriate method for ranking individuals
by their nutritional intakes in epidemiologic studies and has
been validated against 15 24-h food records among participants
in the Rotterdam Study obtaining good correlations between
both methods [ 15,33]. Furthermore, the generalizability of these
results should be taken into account. Our study population is on
average healthier and higher educated compared to the general
population. As subjects with prevalent CHD, stroke and diabetes
at baseline were excluded from the analysis suggesting a higher
risk of developing CHD in these groups, the evaluated study
population is a relatively healthy group. Therefore, results can
only be generalized to a relatively healthy older population.
Additional studies in populations with different social economic
and health status may increase generalizability of these ﬁndings.
Another reason for the null- ﬁndings of this study is that mea-
sures of quality of the macronutrients that we did not capture in
this study determines effect on health rather than quantity.
Previous studies have suggested that quality instead of quantity
of macronutrients, such as carbohydrate, may be a better
determinant for health outcomes [ 34]. Therefore, a focus on
these aspects of nutrition may be more insightful. Still, we did
observe that higher plant protein intake was consistently asso-
ciated with a lower risk of CHD, albeit non-signi ﬁcant. The
reason this association did not reach statistical signi ﬁcance could
be due to the fact that plant protein is simply a re ﬂection of a
higher plant-based diet. However, it could also be explained by
an overall low plant-protein intake in the study population,
making it dif ﬁcult to detect signi ﬁcant associations. Another
explanation may be that different sources of plant protein could
have different effects on the risk of CHD. Future studies exam-
ining the role of different sources of plant protein may help
further elucidate associations between diet and health.
In conclusion, macronutrient composition was not signiﬁcantly
associated with CHD incidence or risk factors in an adult popu-
lation. Food sources and quality of macronutrients may be more
important than quantity, which should be further investigated in
future studies.
